entry.title: Software factories › Measurement & improvement: Don't sloptimize your CI
entry.summary: • Don't sloptimize your CI: Watch the speed of your automated checks: it's easy to sloptimize them until CI slows down the whole factory. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2125561070404428270)

entry.title: Code quality › Codebase structure: Study the cookout repo for code structure
entry.summary: • Study the cookout repo for code structure: Browse github.com/mattpocock/cookout (2,000 commits, not ready yet) to see Matt Pocock's current thinking on how code should be structured. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2125540436483711074)

entry.title: Prompting › Prompt templates: Hunt for implicit state machines
entry.summary: • Hunt for implicit state machines: Tell an agent to look for implicit state machines in your code and the bugs they cause. Charlie Cheever did this on Exact and it found (and fixed) 4 real bugs. (Source: https://x.com/ccheever/status/2125524484857708594)

entry.title: Software factories › Security & identity: Don't let agents act as you
entry.summary: • Don't let agents act as you: Agents that use your identity can send slop people think is yours, do things you didn't want (his assistant answered a password-reset email he hadn't requested), or get prompt-injected into leaking data from your other tools. For factories, sandbox agents and give them service accounts instead of human identities. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2125433860460843443)

entry.title: Workflows › Delegation & agent teams: Agent teams vs. factories: engineer either one
entry.summary: • Agent teams vs. factories: engineer either one: The metaphor matters less than the engineering: agent teams are fine if they're defined in code with metrics, evals, self-improvement loops and benchmarking. Teams and factories can also hand work to each other. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2125427862065025030)

entry.title: Software factories › Architecture & orchestration: How to build a software factory you'll actually use
entry.summary: Article by @BHolmesDev, recommended by Zach Lloyd as the most comprehensive guide he's seen on setting up a software factory from scratch. It grows a plain backlog agent into a factory with a structured blueprint, triage and spec gates for human judgment, computer-use verification, and merge-risk assessment. • Write the factory as a blueprint, not a markdown list: Turn the step list into a YAML blueprint: each stage has a prompt (kept in its own Markdown file), named inputs, structured outputs and a `to` field for where work goes next, and runs on a worker sandbox with its own context (e.g. a foreman that talks to the user and a builder that writes code). Every run returns the same shape of result, and the flow can be visualized. • Label-triggered backlog runs: Start a factory task whenever a GitHub issue gets a `factory` label. For small, well-defined fixes on a native desktop app, runs with an open-weight model cost under a dollar per issue; deeper feature work needed a second look. • Gate implementation with triage and spec stages: Put triage before implementation to route each request: straight to implementation if well defined, to a spec session if it has open product decisions, or just answer it if it's a question. In the spec stage the agent asks its questions first, then writes the product behavior and technical approach; the spec's validation section becomes the checklist for verifying the work. • A UI verification skill with visual proof: Give agents computer use and an app-specific verification skill (how to start the app, connect to DevTools, walk the requested flow, record proof, plus a 'gotchas' list it grows over time). The PR then carries visual proof: the path walked, a recording, and before/after screenshots. • Merge-risk assessment skill: Have the agent score each PR on alignment (matches the issue, no drive-by changes), impact (blast radius, auth/permissions/schema), verification, rollback cost (two-way vs one-way door) and error detection, combined into low/medium/high risk. Ask the implementer to run it before opening the PR so it can fix gaps first. Warp's skill: warp.dev/merge-risk. (Source: https://x.com/BHolmesDev/status/2125351601431089418)

entry.title: Models & evaluation › Benchmarking & evaluation: Pick models, harnesses and skills on evidence
entry.summary: • Pick models, harnesses and skills on evidence: Don't choose models, harnesses and skills on vibes or public benchmarks alone. Run the same kinds of tasks on your own codebase through different configurations, compare quality and cost, look at where each succeeds and fails, and keep testing as the tools change. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2125348752814932162)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Personal admin & money: Grok Bot finds, files and gets approval for an unclaimed-money claim
entry.summary: 20-second recap video (made by Evan Bacon's Motion Bot) of Grok Bot running his unclaimed-money prompt: it checks state lists, reports $315.73 across two properties in Texas, files the claim after he says "Do it", and Texas approves it 21 minutes after the search started. The prompt itself is in an earlier card (Prompt: find and claim your unclaimed money). • Event-triggered recap videos: Evan Bacon's Motion Bot made the recap video on its own: the claim approval arriving about 20 minutes after filing triggered it. • 0:03 Unclaimed money: review the matches, then say "Do it": After the unclaimed-money prompt, Grok Bot checks each state's list, then shows what it found before filing: here $315.73 across two Texas properties, plus how to claim (file with a photo ID). The claim only went in after the reply "Do it". • 0:08 Have a photo ID ready for the filing step: Expect the filing step to need a photo ID upload. In this run Texas approved the claim the same day: 21 minutes from search to approval (8:39 to 9:00 AM). (Source: https://x.com/Baconbrix/status/2125272594828103712)

entry.title: Software factories › Architecture & orchestration: PR attribution for agent work
entry.summary: • PR attribution for agent work: Warp's model: on human-initiated PRs the human is the author, the agent is the reviewer, and the human merges (agent-as-author broke tooling and removed human responsibility). Fully automated PRs have the agent as author. For PRs from a multi-person Slack or Jira thread, the original prompter is the author and commits are attributed across collaborators. Make it configurable. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2125264800175260039)

entry.title: Software factories › Measurement & improvement: Measure whether agents make you better, not just busier
entry.summary: • Measure whether agents make you better, not just busier: Look across the workflow: how long work takes, how much is automated, what a PR costs, how much business value it adds, and where agents spend time on work that doesn't help. More PRs isn't the goal; record agent runs and measure results so you can tune and improve them. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2125243114948599941)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Directory & templates: Editing and refreshing your grok-bot.directory listing
entry.summary: Replies from Eric Zakariasson explaining the new edit and refresh controls for community apps on grok-bot.directory, and how official apps differ. • Edit your community listing on grok-bot.directory: Sign in to grok-bot.directory with GitHub (the account that submitted the app), open your submissions and hit Edit to change its name, description, logo and website. A new name or description reruns the security check, so the listing is hidden for a few minutes. If the app isn't in your list, claim it from its page first. • Refresh re-reads plugin.json; set displayName: The directory doesn't pull changes on its own: Refresh in your submissions re-reads your repo's plugin.json and follows renames and moves. To show a friendlier name (e.g. "PR Genie"), add displayName to plugin.json and hit Refresh. • Official apps: edit the marketplace's .cursor-plugin/plugin.json: Official apps mirror the marketplace catalog and can't be claimed on the directory. The marketplace reads .cursor-plugin/plugin.json, not .grok-plugin/plugin.json, so change the description there; it syncs to the directory overnight. (Source: https://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2124941358339178841)

entry.title: Software factories › Architecture & orchestration: Define your factory in shared code
entry.summary: • Define your factory in shared code: Don't keep coding-agent setup in someone's head or on one laptop. Define the agents, their roles, skills, triggers and workflow in shared code so the factory is versioned: test a change on a branch, see what changed, roll back if it gets worse. An agent can even spot a recurring failure and propose a change to the factory definition. Aim for a system you can improve, not a perfect day-one config. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2124986381470707937)

entry.title: Workflows › Planning & process: 12 Rules for a Software Factory That Doesn't Ship Slop — Dex Horthy (AI Engineer)
entry.summary: 20-minute AI Engineer Code Summit talk ('12-Factor Factories & The War on Slop'). Dex Horthy compares a 2022-style software factory with an agentic one, walks through twelve practices for factories that don't ship slop (planning, visual alignment, testing tools, deterministic lint rules, experiments, evals, a unified forge), and closes by reading the Anti-Slop Manifesto. • 6:00 Loops = forward pressure + backpressure: Design factory loops with both forward pressure (work starts on its own) and backpressure (agents keep iterating against quality checks) so output reaches a high bar before a human reviews it. • 9:27 Plan before agents build: Bring back architecture reviews and sprint-style planning before agents write code: about 30 minutes of alignment up front can save hours of review and rework later. • 10:07 Size planning by expected pain: Don't over-plan. Weigh expected pain (chance you'll have to redo it × how painful the change is): a two-sentence prompt is fine for low-stakes work, while core database changes deserve detailed schemas up front. • 11:00 Align visually, not with walls of text: Have agents produce visual artifacts such as HTML mockups, charts or tables instead of long text, so humans can quickly understand and agree on a design, before the build or after. • 11:24 Give agents a way to test their own work: Let agents run the app where it actually lives and check the result with screenshots, a browser, video or cURL. For a mobile app, give them a sandbox where they can build, run and see what happened. • 11:38 Fight slop with deterministic tools: Don't rely only on AI reviewing AI. Strict linters, type checkers and custom lint rules stop agents from merging known-bad patterns every time. • 12:09 Slop is a tool: Unreviewed, imperfect output is fine where stakes are low: quick prototypes, side projects, or experiments kept behind feature flags. • 12:24 Let models run experiments: Connect agents to your feature-flag and A/B testing tools (the slide names PostHog and Statsig) so they can try variations and let real metrics pick the winner. • 12:36 Compound: eval everything, learn from past sessions: Run evals on everything and feed lessons from past sessions back into the system so the factory gets better over time. • 12:40 Unify your forge: Keep designs, decisions and docs in one source of truth (such as GitHub) instead of scattered Slack threads and docs, so humans and agents share the same context. • 13:25 You can't buy a factory: A software factory is a way of working, not a product. You can buy infrastructure, but you still have to tune the rules and governance to your own codebase and team. (Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-NFMsM2y0Vk)

entry.title: Prompting › Prompt templates: Replacing an 18-tab compensation spreadsheet with a Droid-built app
entry.summary: 61-second demo by @troymartig, recommended by Eno Reyes: one prompt to Factory's Droid builds a compensation tracker from the Rippling API, checks its numbers against the source system, publishes a web app, runs daily at 7am and Slacks a summary, with a final human Approve step for the pay run. • 0:14 One prompt that specifies the whole job: Spell out the whole job in one prompt: data source, business logic, output, schedule and notification. The demo prompt: "Build us a compensation tracker. Pull our employees straight from the Rippling API, work out what each person is owed by month in their own currency, and tie it all out across our systems. Publish it as a web app, run it daily at 7am, and once the checks pass, Slack me what changed." • 0:23 Make the agent tie out numbers against the source system: Ask the agent to "tie out" its results across systems. In the demo it writes a check like assert ledger.total() == rippling.total() so the generated numbers are verified against the source of truth instead of reviewed by hand. • 0:54 Automate the run, keep a one-click human approval: Let the scheduled agent pull data, detect changes, run its checks and send a Slack summary, then stop at one human step: the pay run waits for an Approve click once every check has passed. (Source: https://x.com/troymartig/status/2124920941474193755)

entry.title: Software factories › Concepts & adoption: Software factories vs. agent teams
entry.summary: Zach Lloyd contrasts two visions: software factories (code-defined, closed-loop systems that measure and improve cloud coding agents) and agent teams that individuals manage, and argues the factory approach fits the real problem better. • Treat agent deployment as an optimization problem: Frame the goal as securely deploying coding agents to maximize throughput and quality at minimum cost. That chain forces the design: optimizing needs measurement, measurement needs reliable standardized data, that needs centralization, so move agents to the cloud, define the factory in code, keep it open to try different models, harnesses and skills, and feed what you learn back in. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2124903221621612762)

entry.title: Software factories › Concepts & adoption: What counts as a software factory
entry.summary: • What counts as a software factory: Agent swarms, shared skills and collections of automations can be useful, but a software factory is a code-defined, closed-loop system that runs coding agents, measures how they perform and improves them over time. Declarative beats imperative: define the system in code so you can test, measure and improve it. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2124880726877421813)

entry.title: Workflows › Delegation & agent teams: A shared chat workspace for agents and developers
entry.summary: • A shared chat workspace for agents and developers: Vercel Board is basically a private Slack workspace where your agents and developers work together, and it can sync to Slack channels for observability. Matt Pocock thinks most teams should build their own version from scratch. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2124797717834543167)

entry.title: Models & evaluation › Benchmarking & evaluation: If you don't read the code, read the evals
entry.summary: • If you don't read the code, read the evals: Models are still bad at writing and code-reviewing evals. If you don't read the code an agent writes, at least read its evals. (Source: https://x.com/dexhorthy/status/2124666271530995771)

entry.title: Prompting › Steering & context: Code mode (PTC) for a daily Linear sweep
entry.summary: Dex Horthy on a code-mode hack (Procedural Tool Calling) in Factory that cut a daily Linear sweep's tokens and run time, plus a follow-up reply on why it works. • Code mode cut a daily Linear sweep from 245k to 23k tokens: Using Procedural Tool Calling (basically code mode, where the agent writes code that calls the tools) in Factory dropped a daily Linear sweep from 245k tokens to 23k and from 7 minutes to 36 seconds. • Show the model only the fields that drive the decision: Most of the code-mode win comes from making sure the model only sees the Linear fields that matter to its decisions, instead of the giant blobs of JSON tool calls usually return. (Source: https://x.com/dexhorthy/status/2124624191563698426)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Harnesses & tools: Keep the lab's tool defs and system prompt; own the rest
entry.summary: • Keep the lab's tool defs and system prompt; own the rest: Don't use a lab's harness blindly, but its tool definitions and system prompt are part of how the model was RL'd, so if you depart from them you're on your own. Other parts of the harness, like orchestration, are yours to own. (Source: https://x.com/dexhorthy/status/2124613833050472826)

entry.title: Software factories › Measurement & improvement: Benchmarking subagents vs. one agent in Warp's software factory
entry.summary: 6:47 screen recording: Zach Lloyd walks through Warp's internal factory (a triage → spec → implementation → code-review → delivery blueprint defined in factory.yaml), then benchmarks a version with a dedicated subagent per stage against a single agent running the same stages in one context window. • 2:12 Write stage transitions as plain-language conditions: Factory stage transitions don't have to be rigid if/then code. Warp's factory.yaml describes when each stage applies in plain English (e.g. stay in triage while "the cause, scope, or tracking state is not yet known") and lets the agent decide when to move on. • 3:51 Benchmark factory designs by replaying real past tasks: Build a benchmark from real coding tasks your team already completed and replay them through each factory configuration, measuring correctness and cost, instead of picking an agent architecture from opinions online. • 5:26 Per-stage subagents cost ~40% more for no real quality gain: On Warp's benchmark, giving each factory stage its own subagent (own context window and computer) averaged $6.27 per task versus $3.84 for one agent running the same stages in a single context window, about 40% more expensive with no meaningful quality gain. The single-agent setup became their default; don't assume subagents pay off until your own benchmark shows it. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2124592480674779605)

entry.title: Prompting › Prompt templates: A pstack prompt for gardening your codebase
entry.summary: • A pstack prompt for gardening your codebase: Run "Use /poteto-mode on this repo", then have it find the mistakes agents and humans keep repeating (git log, past bug fixes, review comments) and make each impossible: architecture first, then types, then a lint whose error names the fix, then a test. Delete comments that restate code (/no-comments), write formal models that replay past concurrency/retry/state-machine bugs (/create-formal-verification-skill) and run them in CI, replace implementation-pinning unit tests with those models plus real DB and e2e tests (keeping security and legal tests), and ship one verifiable PR per step. (Source: https://x.com/poteto/status/2124525336994177412)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Skill packs & updates: VECTOR: a /vector skill for delegating any task to AI
entry.summary: Matt Pocock is writing docs for VECTOR, a skill for non-developers that guides you through delegating a task to AI in six steps. The docs aren't released yet. • /vector: six steps to delegate a task to AI: VECTOR is a skill (/vector) for non-developers that walks you through delegating a task to AI in six steps: find workflows AI could help with, give agents the right context, reorder the workflow, and find ways it can improve over time through memory. Planned docs include the /vector skill for building your own workflows, workshop templates for helping people new to AI build theirs, and example prompts. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2124471135953723528)

entry.title: Prompting › Steering & context: Teaching an agent your writing style with a sentence scorer
entry.summary: A short self-thread on getting an agent to learn your writing style by scoring its sentences one at a time, with a follow-up on which scoring mode worked better. • Sentence-scorer loop for your writing style: To get an agent to write in your style, build a small 'scorer' app where the agent sends you example sentences one at a time and you score them swipe-left style. Plan an article together, work through it sentence by sentence, and let the agent test its own hypotheses about your style and build up a profile over time. • Review sentence by sentence: Working sentence by sentence fits the small amount of high-quality working memory people have: instead of judging whether a whole piece flows together, you only judge whether one sentence reads well. • Score one sentence at a time, not pick-the-best: In the scorer, single mode ("score this sentence 1-4") worked far better than multi ("which of these is better"). Reading three options and choosing the best is much harder on your brain than giving fast, vibes-based feedback on one. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2124214098984370645)

entry.title: Workflows › Planning & process: Plan up front only when rework is costly
entry.summary: • Plan up front only when rework is costly: Up-front planning with an agent pays off when rework is costly, such as large diffs and features. When rework is cheap, there's not much need for it. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2124147482238333210)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Alignment & domain docs: Record hard-won naming decisions in ADRs
entry.summary: • Record hard-won naming decisions in ADRs: When a grilling session settles a naming or data-relationship question (his example ADR: "A Thumbnail Diagram is not a Diagram"), write it up as an ADR; without it the agent would fill the gap with its own assumptions. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2124058139477594142)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Releases & features: Grok Bot Q&A - Travel, 1.0, meetings & more! (X broadcast)
entry.summary: Friday jam livestream on what's new in Grok Bot: travel search, phone calls and meetings, tool permissions, the Directory, memory import, plus community workflows shown on screen. • 6:52 Search flights in chat: Ask for flights in plain words (the demo: "Find nonstop flights from SFO to LAX"); Grok Bot answers with a short pick plus Recommended and Cheapest option cards. • 9:51 Phone calls from Grok Bot: Grok Bot can make phone calls: call a business, use calls as a tool, hand a call off to you, confirm who it's calling, and show a live transcript. • 18:30 Per-tool permissions on connector pages: On a connector's page, set each tool to Always allow, Auto-review, Needs approval or Blocked to control exactly what the bot may run without you. • 27:37 Don't run one chat forever: Using the same bot chat for too long degrades results because it has to re-read the whole chat; spin up fresh bots or split tasks instead. • 31:10 Install community bots from the Directory: The Grok Bot Directory lists community-built bot templates you can install instead of building from scratch. • 46:22 Import memory from another assistant: Settings has an "Import memory to Grok Bot" page: click Start import to bring your preferences, context and memories over from another AI assistant. (Source: https://x.com/i/broadcasts/2aWQllRAKjNOBd)

entry.title: Code quality › Lint rules & bans: Try pstack's /no-comments, or turn it into a lint rule
entry.summary: • Try pstack's /no-comments, or turn it into a lint rule: Run the /no-comments skill from pstack (github.com/cursor/plugins, pstack/skills/no-comments), or better, ask your agent to turn it into a lint rule. (Source: https://x.com/poteto/status/2123898792487576021)

entry.title: Software factories › Measurement & improvement: Engineer Your Coding Agents Like Any Other System — Zach Lloyd, Warp
entry.summary: AI Engineer Code Summit keynote: software engineering is becoming factory engineering. Lloyd lays out a code-defined, closed-loop factory stack (declarative definition, recorded agent runs, sandboxed compute, flexible inference, online evals, self-improvement PRs, benchmarks on your own data); from about 10:40 it becomes a Warp Factories product demo. • 3:56 Encode the factory declaratively: Define your factory in a declarative, version-controlled language (like Terraform): which agents run, how they're triggered, their workflows and the tools they can use. • 7:28 Product engineering vs. factory engineering: Building the product and improving the system of agents that builds it are two distinct skill sets; treat factory engineering as its own job. • 9:00 Record everything agents produce: Centrally record agent conversations, artifacts, videos and screenshots; that record is the raw material for improving the factory. • 9:37 Keep the inference layer flexible: Run agents in sandboxes for security and repeatability, and support multiple models and agent harnesses, since different tasks need different capabilities. • 13:24 Online evals score agent output: Have separate agents review and score your coding agents' output as it happens (e.g. flag redundant or unnecessary tests) to catch failure modes. • 14:59 Self-improvement as PRs: Let agents read the eval scores, find failure patterns, and propose fixes as pull requests against the factory's own definition. • 15:51 Benchmark on your own tasks: Skip generic leaderboards: build a benchmark from your organization's real past tasks and replay it across models and configurations to weigh quality against cost. (Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LeT996Hz3E)

entry.title: Code quality › Comments & docs: Put the 'why' in ADRs, not comments
entry.summary: • Put the 'why' in ADRs, not comments: Comments are a bad store for the why of a codebase, so put it in an ADR instead. Not every piece of code needs one, and don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2123861337650471082)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Alignment & domain docs: ADRs stop agents re-suggesting explored avenues
entry.summary: • ADRs stop agents re-suggesting explored avenues: ADRs keep agents from repeatedly recommending approaches you've already explored, and let them see the history of surprising decisions after you hand the system off. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2123860812607758629)

entry.title: Workflows › Remixable software: voiced: open-source dictation, remixed by prompt
entry.summary: 18-second demo: one voiced dictation pill is forked again and again by prompt into an orb, a green terminal, a VU meter, a pirate-voice cleanup and more. • 0:00 Fork-and-remix prompt for voiced: voiced (github.com/ericzakariasson/voiced) is an open-source dictation and voice-prompting tool powered by Grok voice. To customize it, prompt your agent: "Fork Voiced, read AGENTS.md at its root and follow its first run section, then make this change: …" (e.g. make the pill hot pink, or make the cleanup talk like a pirate). (Source: https://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2123825984231362902)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Skill packs & updates: pstack updates itself; rerun /setup-pstack to change routing
entry.summary: • pstack updates itself; rerun /setup-pstack to change routing: pstack v0.15.46 prunes its skills to be much shorter and adds Gemini 4 Neon as a panel reviewer. It auto-updates for Grok Bot and Cursor users; to change which models handle which role, run /setup-pstack again. (Source: https://x.com/poteto/status/2123824683862855898)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Alignment & domain docs: Only document what won't churn
entry.summary: • Only document what won't churn: Low-granularity docs that rarely change (high-level system architecture, one sentence on each package's role) are safe; beyond that, keeping a second copy of the truth tends to slow agents and humans down. Agents that fight doc drift for you have rarely been worth the trouble over a couple of months. (Source: https://x.com/dexhorthy/status/2123816567259697401)

entry.title: Software factories › Concepts & adoption: Factories vs. agent teams
entry.summary: • Factories vs. agent teams: Treat deploying coding agents as an optimization problem: you can only optimize what you measure, measurement needs standardized data, and that needs a centralized, code-defined factory in the cloud that lets you test different models, harnesses and skills and feed learnings back in. Agent teams that you manage like people lack that measurement loop. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2123808803070063033)

entry.title: Software factories › Concepts & adoption: Hands-on software factory course
entry.summary: • Hands-on software factory course: Warp's team published a hands-on introductory course on learning about and building your own software factory at warp.dev/learn. (Source: https://x.com/zachlloydtweets/status/2123805046307430871)

entry.title: Prompting › Prompt templates: Comment-audit prompt
entry.summary: • Comment-audit prompt: Ask the agent to categorise every code comment in your codebase (or one section) as Tautology (repeats the code), Excuse (lets a hacky implementation slide), Stale (refers to code that no longer applies) or Decision Record (an important, non-obvious decision). Then: delete tautologies and stale comments, delete excuses and file an issue to fix the hack, and move decision records into ADRs. • Ban comments with a ratchet, then make it a skill: After the cleanup, have the agent add a lint rule banning comments with a ratchet approach (not every comment goes in one PR), create a /delete-comment skill in the repo so you can repeat the process, and estimate how many lines you'll shed. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2123798388227403983)

entry.title: Code quality › Review & judgment: 'There will always be alpha in reviewing something': No Slop Manifesto talk excerpt (via @aiDotEngineer)
entry.summary: As models improve, shift review from line-by-line code to plans, designs and outcomes; bring your own thinking or you get the same baseline output as everyone. Slop is fine when it gets you to the outcome, bad when it hurts quality, maintainability or teammates' time. • 0:16 Scale human review to the stakes: Agent reviewers, linters and verifiers help but aren't enough; scale human review to the stakes, not to lines of code or PR counts. • 0:34 Slop is fine when it gets you the outcome: One-shot prompts and vibe coding are fine when they get you the outcome; slop is bad only when it undermines quality, maintainability or teammates' time. (Source: https://x.com/aiDotEngineer/status/2123566998294601980)

entry.title: Software factories › Concepts & adoption: Introducing Warp Learn: build a software factory (via @warpdotdev)
entry.summary: Warp Learn / Warp Factories overview: workflows defined as YAML, quality and cost dashboards, a self-improvement toggle, and built-in benchmarking. • Free course: build your own software factory (Warp Learn): Warp Learn is a free, hands-on course (taught by @BHolmesDev) that goes from fundamentals to a first automation loop to a full factory with specs, risk assessment and end-to-end verification. Zach's definition: an automation loop in the cloud that orchestrates agents to build better software over time. • 0:27 Warp Factories: workflows as YAML, dashboards, self-improvement: Define agent workflows as code in YAML; dashboards track code quality, test coverage, regression risk and cost per PR (00:51); a Self-Improvement toggle lets the loop optimize itself (00:58); built-in benchmarking compares configs, subagents and models (01:03). (Source: https://x.com/warpdotdev/status/2123493996286951624)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Shopping & travel: Plan your next trip with Grok Bot (via @bot)
entry.summary: Demo: asking Grok Bot for specific flights and themed hotel options, and picking from bookable choices in chat. • Give travel bookings loose preferences, not exact specs: Grok Bot can book seats, rebook a missed connection, help with refunds, or watch for upgrades, often triggered automatically from email. Pro tip: state loose preferences (for example, that you prefer aisle seats and don't mind waiting longer) rather than exact details and it generally finds better options. • 0:19 Give travel requests themes and dates: Ask for specific flights (e.g. nonstop SFO to LAX) and pick from options in chat (00:05), or give themed preferences and dates (e.g. a desert hotel near Joshua Tree) to get bookable hotel options. (Source: https://x.com/bot/status/2123121401762918718)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Alignment & domain docs: Watch me work: building a 21,000-line PR with /grill-with-docs and /retro
entry.summary: Matt Pocock builds a thumbnail-editor feature for his Course Video Manager app with Claude Code in VS Code. He aligns with the agent first (/grill-with-docs), pins down domain language in GLOSSARY.md plus an ADR, compacts the planning chat into a spec and tickets, runs /implement-spec to get one large PR, then runs /retro so the agent reviews its own work against project standards (it flags ignored rules, too many comments, and a PR too big to review) and splits it into smaller stacked PRs that he reviews and merges one at a time. Matt also offers a free email course on his skills (aihero.dev/skills/subscribe). • Prefer soft deletes when replacing an old system: Use a soft delete (e.g. an archived flag) instead of hard-deleting data, so you can revert. • 3:08 Choose the approach by change size: One-shot tiny changes; for big features, start with an alignment phase on domain language. • 4:43 Grill first: let the agent question you before coding: A command like /grill-with-docs makes the agent ask you questions before it writes any code. • 10:29 Keep a GLOSSARY.md of project terms: Agents write better code when they know your domain's nouns and verbs. • 16:18 Record ADRs so agents don't undo past decisions: Architectural Decision Records tell the agent why past decisions were made. • 26:30 Compact the planning chat into a spec and tickets: Before implementing, compact a long planning chat (/compact) into a clean spec and a list of tickets, then run /implement-spec. • 58:33 Run /retro after a big generation: The agent reviews its own code against your standards for rule violations, scope creep and excess complexity. • 1:01:03 Split a huge PR into stacked PRs: Have the agent break a big PR into smaller stacked PRs (e.g. schema, backend, UI) and review them one by one. (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2123098316867051991)

entry.title: Models & evaluation › Benchmarking & evaluation: Emergent Behaviors with Gabe Orlanski, creator of SlopCodeBench: AI That Works #81 (X broadcast)
entry.summary: @dexhorthy hosts Gabe Orlanski (creator of SlopCodeBench, University of Wisconsin) and Vaibhav (@vaibcode, BoundaryML founder). SlopCodeBench tests agents on iterative, multi-checkpoint tasks: agents solve isolated steps but fail to refactor or centralize code as requirements grow, piling on workarounds. Gabe's post "Slop is Moving Up the Stack" adds that agents rewrite libraries instead of using provided ones, and LibraryDesignBench shows agent-designed libraries are hard for other agents to use. Recurring anti-patterns: Go-style (value, error) returns in Python, catch-and-reraise at every layer, and type(x) == T instead of isinstance(). • 10:20 Evaluate agents on multi-step iterative tasks: One-shot tests miss it: watch whether agents refactor and centralize code as requirements grow, or pile on workarounds. • 14:50 Watch for library avoidance: Agents often rewrite provided libraries from scratch instead of using them. • 17:00 Judge an agent-designed API by whether other agents can use it: LibraryDesignBench finds agent-designed libraries are often hard for other agents to use. • 21:20 Python anti-patterns agents produce: Watch for Go-style (value, error) tuple returns in Python (21:20), catch-and-reraise at every layer instead of letting exceptions bubble up (22:20), and type(x) == T instead of isinstance() (24:25). • 32:50 For big refactors, delete and reimplement from a new plan: For a big refactor or library swap, delete the old code and tests, have the agent write a new plan, and reimplement from scratch rather than editing in place. (Source: https://x.com/i/broadcasts/2WXPoPRqBdVEPZ)

entry.title: Cursor › Voice prompts: Cursor: voice prompts straight to the agent (demo)
entry.summary: Demo of dictating prompts to the Cursor agent with the mic button: live transcription, editing before sending, and use for follow-ups. • Send voice prompts straight to the agent: New in Cursor: voice prompts can go directly to the agent, without a separate click to dictate and another to send. Built by a self-described voice-prompting power user. • 0:07 Edit dictated prompts before sending, including follow-ups: Click the mic in the agent prompt box to dictate (text transcribes live); cancel or stop recording and edit before sending. It works for follow-ups too, e.g. 'Write a unit test for the dark mode toggle' (00:22). (Source: https://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2122419926208249898)

entry.title: Prompting › Steering & context: LIVE: Writing code that doesn't suck with the creators of Pi (with @badlogicgames and @mitsuhiko)
entry.summary: Matt Pocock talks with Armin Ronacher (@mitsuhiko) and Mario Zechner (@badlogicgames), the creators of Pi, about where coding agents help and where they don't. Agents are strong tactically (fast code, reliable bug triage) but weak at system design, architecture and ambiguous problems. Use the time agents save on drudgery for quality rather than more features, and keep humans on domain knowledge, trade-offs and oversight. • 7:35 Use a field's precise domain terms in prompts: Precise domain vocabulary pulls the relevant knowledge out of the model. • 8:12 Tell the model which trade-offs matter: The model's first correct solution is rarely the best one; state the trade-offs that matter for your problem. • 8:41 Give agents straight-line tasks toward a verifiable goal: Agents are strong tactically but weak at ambiguous design work that needs judgment; hand them clear tasks with a verifiable goal. • 9:08 Avoid nuance in the APIs and codebases agents work in: Ambiguity leads agents to poor choices and slop. • 12:20 Spend the time agents save on quality: Use the time saved on drudgery to raise quality, not just to ship more features. • 28:30 Re-check agent code's assumptions as data grows: Trade-offs chosen early (e.g. for an empty database) can break as data grows; revisit them over time. (Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZBTegd8DUZM)

entry.title: Prompting › Steering & context: Intra-turn interaction: AI UX beyond turn-taking (via @liu_xingyu)
entry.summary: Intra-turn, feedforward UX: the AI surfaces its assumptions as editable widgets before generating, so you can steer without extra chat turns. • 0:04 Surface assumptions as editable widgets before generating: Feedforward UX: the AI shows its assumptions (e.g. kids' ages, interests) as editable controls before writing the plan, offers preselected style/color dropdowns for creative assets (00:26), and 'leaving blanks' templates for missing details like guest count or tone (00:41), so you steer without extra chat turns. (Source: https://x.com/liu_xingyu/status/2121015724374397183)

entry.title: Code quality › Lint rules & bans: All Code Is Slop (Except Mine), Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI (AIE Code talk)
entry.summary: Lauren Tan (@poteto) on scaling Grok Bot's coding agents into a high-trust "software factory". Agents learn from their environment, so remove bad patterns, ban nuanced APIs, and replace prose instructions and code comments with strict architectural boundaries and lint rules. Spend most agent effort on programmatic verification (custom app CLIs, formal proofs, property-based UI tests) so agents verify their own work before human review. Results shown: 10,926 PRs merged in October (of 23,310 total), 19 desktop releases a month with a median 23 hours between releases, a revert rate steady at 0.47%, and comments cut from 65,824 to 1,227 while lint rules grew to 169. • 2:02 Guide agents with an inverted pyramid: deterministic first, prose last: Rely most on deterministic codebase design and static analysis (API design, architecture, lint rules, types, tests), then verification, and least on prose instructions (rules, skills, AGENTS.md) and human review. • 3:09 Turn every agent correction into a deterministic check: When you correct an agent, or catch something in review, make the fix a lint rule or other deterministic check in the codebase rather than new text in an instructions markdown file. Agents copy the patterns they see, so keep bad patterns out of the code. • 4:57 Enforce architecture with directory-based import bans: Encode boundaries in the directory structure and ban imports across them, e.g. code in electron-renderer can't import from electron-main. • 5:25 Design foolproof APIs; ban nuanced ones like useEffect: APIs that need nuance to use well lead to slop. Design foolproof APIs and ban nuanced ones, such as React's useEffect in product code. • 6:55 Stop agents writing unsolicited markdown docs: Agents use markdown and docs they weren't asked for to justify wrong implementations; stop them writing it. • 7:22 Ban imperative quick fixes like setTimeout and requestAnimationFrame: Quick fixes spread: in the example shown, one agent's timer hack grew to 183 timers. Ban imperative timer-based patches such as setTimeout/requestAnimationFrame. • 8:19 Treat code comments as liabilities: Comments aren't enforceable and agents use them to justify workarounds, so delete them. The team cut comments from 65,824 to 1,227 while growing to 169 lint rules. • 9:34 Give runtime-verification skills a feature map: Runtime-verification skills include a 'feature map': a user-facing site map of the app's features, giving agents and humans shared vocabulary (so 'the thingy in the left sidebar' is unambiguous), plus reusable custom CLIs/drivers that save tokens and are testable. • 10:01 Spend most agent tokens on verification, with an app CLI to drive the app: Put roughly 70% of agent token spend into verification. Give agents a CLI to drive and screenshot your app so they check their own work before human review, e.g. `app aria:click --accessible-name "Settings"`, `app snapshot`, `app screenshot proof.png`. • 10:49 Model state machines with TLA+ and prove algorithms with Lean: Add formal verification as another layer: TLA+ to model state machines and Lean to prove algorithms. • 11:34 Fuzz your UI with property-based testing (Bombadil): Use property-based UI testing to fuzz the UI; the Grok Bot team uses Bombadil (github.com/antithesishq/bombadil). • 12:54 Generate statecharts and other visual artifacts for reviewers: Have agents produce visual artifacts such as statecharts so reviewers can check behavior quickly. The statechart skill is part of pstack (github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack). • 15:48 Don't automate a low-trust loop: If your inner agent loop produces slop, automating it just produces more. Improve constraints and self-verification first. • 16:06 Once the loop is high-trust, add an outer loop on triggers: With a trusted inner loop, add an outer loop that kicks off agents from Linear tickets, Slack messages, cron schedules, or Datadog/Sentry alerts. • 16:15 Example outer loop: auto-fuzz every release with Grok Bot: On each new release, Grok Bot spins up a Cursor project that fuzzes the build like a real user, opens fix PRs for bugs it finds, and auto-merges them. (Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O_zcc6Xl12g)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Meetings: Grok Bot can now join meetings (via @bot; also quoted by @Baconbrix)
entry.summary: Demo: ask your bot in chat to join an in-progress Zoom or Google Meet call; it takes spoken requests and writes structured notes and action items into apps like Notion. • Bring your bot to meetings so it gathers its own context: Inviting a bot to meetings lets it collect context firsthand, which makes it smarter over time. It can also attend for you (e.g. when you're on a flight without connectivity) and take notes. To set it up, just ask your bot. • 0:16 Ask the bot for things out loud during meetings: Once in a Zoom/Google Meet call (ask it in chat to join), the bot responds to spoken requests such as sending follow-ups, confirms with a chat reaction, and writes structured notes and action items into apps like Notion (00:18). (Source: https://x.com/bot/status/2121320089920430181)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Links & docs: Ask Grok Bot questions in the docs (demo)
entry.summary: Demo of 'Ask Grok Bot' on a docs page, answering a question about how Grok Bot handles a task with a step-by-step flowchart. • Ask Grok Bot questions inside the docs: The docs (docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview) now have Grok Bot built in: it answers from the docs, links the pages it used, and can draw a diagram of how a task runs. • 0:00 Ask the docs for a diagram: On supported docs pages, 'Ask Grok Bot' answers questions about the page; asking it to walk through how Grok Bot handles a task 'with a diagram' returns a step-by-step flowchart. (Source: https://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2121294195843629360)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Review & explainer skills: /animatic skill preview: videos instead of walls of markdown
entry.summary: Work-in-progress skill that turns a PR into a short narrated video so humans can review agent PRs faster. • Swap walls of markdown for an /animatic video: Matt is building two skills: /setup-animatic (picks the tooling and sets it up locally or on a remote machine) and /animatic (creates an upload-ready video). The goal: every important PR comes with a video showing how it works. • 0:14 How /animatic turns a PR into a narrated video: The agent writes a JSON storyboard, Playwright renders code frames from the PR diff, TTS reads each line and FFmpeg stitches an MP4. Voice engine (ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Edge-TTS), rendering style and stitcher are CLI options (00:56); the MP4 is posted as a PR comment via the GitHub/GitLab API or saved locally (01:25). (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2121211579098083668)

Put one in a shortcut, a note, or another app. Build your own with the deep-links docs at docs.x.ai/grok-bot/deep-links. • 0:00 Prefill links come in web and app forms: Shareable prefilled-prompt links work as a web link (https://cursor.com/grok-bot/link/v1/prompt?text=...) or an app link (grokbot://app/v1/prompt?text=...). (Source: https://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2120959534537871653)

entry.title: Mobile & app building › Cloud simulators: Introducing Expo Simulators: cloud simulators built for agents (via @expo)
entry.summary: Cloud Android/iOS simulators that let AI agents visually verify app changes, usable from local and cloud agents, with an optional pause for a human check before shipping. • Let agents verify mobile changes on cloud simulators: Expo Simulators are cloud simulators/emulators built for agents: the agent runs its change on one and brings back a recording before asking for your attention, which helps when agents write mobile code faster than a team can review. • 0:36 Let agents check UI across device types, with a human pause: Expo Simulators work from local and cloud agents (00:25), let agents test UI across iPhones, Androids, foldables and watches, and the workflow can pause for a human to check the simulator before the agent ships (00:50). (Source: https://x.com/expo/status/2120924979898601506)

entry.title: Grok Bot › Teams & delegation: Introducing Grok Bot 1.0: AI teammates (via @bot)
entry.summary: Grok Bot 1.0 as AI teammates: specialized bots (e.g. research, copy, deck) collaborate in chats, calls and design tools, hand work to each other, and flag risks before content is shared. • Delegate whole workstreams, not just personal errands: Grok Bot isn't just a personal agent: treat it as a teammate you can hand full workstreams to and let it run them end to end. Grok Bot 1.0 added sharing bots, working with them in Slack and Teams, and inviting them to meetings. • 0:09 Pull a bot into a video call from chat: Invite a bot to a video call from text chat and it joins. • 0:35 Have bots tag each other to hand off work: Bots can tag one another in channels to pass work along (e.g. a research bot handing off to a copy bot). • 0:55 Use a bot as a safety net before sharing: Bots can warn you about sensitive content, e.g. confidential financials on slides, before a deck is shared externally. (Source: https://x.com/bot/status/2120582957782200586)

entry.title: Agent skills & setup › Home Repo & multi-repo: The Home Repo pattern: working with agents across multiple repos
entry.summary: Keep one central Home Repo holding all agent skills, tooling, docs and config, always run agent sessions from it, and let it reach into your other repos, so capabilities stay in sync across the team. • 2:54 Put private skills and shared settings in the Home Repo: Keep private skills (sensitive workflows) and version-controlled config like settings.json in the Home Repo so the whole team gets them. • 6:36 Keep custom CLI tooling in the Home Repo: E.g. one CLI wrapping Slack, Discord, GitHub and Google Calendar for your agents. The Home Repo can also hold an LLM wiki of markdown on audiences, business concepts and architecture (05:44). (Source: https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2120847219788308872)

entry.title: Models & evaluation › Benchmarking & evaluation: Benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon in Warp Factories (via @warpdotdev)
entry.summary: Demo: running multiple model configurations (Gemini 4 Carbon vs Gemini 4 Argon) in one benchmark on the same harness. • Benchmark new models on your own past agent tasks: When a new model comes out, don't rely on SOTA benchmark numbers: rerun it against your own previous agent tasks to compare cost and quality, and switch only if it measures up. That's why factories should be measurable and model-agnostic. • 0:02 Benchmark several model configs in one run on the same harness: Put multiple model configurations (e.g. Gemini 4 Carbon vs Gemini 4 Argon) in a single benchmark run on the same harness. (Source: https://x.com/warpdotdev/status/2120702943003574441)

entry.title: Testing & verification › Code review agents: How to fix the code review bottleneck (full walkthrough), @BHolmesDev
entry.summary: Ben Holmes (@BHolmesDev) fixes the code review bottleneck in three stages using Warp Factories: an isolated agent-to-agent review loop, end-to-end verification in a sandbox with recorded video, and an automated merge-risk assessment added to the PR description, so humans see polished, verified PRs with a risk summary. In a Warp benchmark shown, an independent reviewer averaged $12.02 and 71.1% correctness vs $4.82 and 68.6% for self-review. • 4:18 Build and own a custom review agent: Write a review agent that enforces your own architecture, PII handling and style rules rather than relying only on off-the-shelf reviewers. • 7:51 Review in a fresh context, not self-review: Hand the diff to a separate reviewer sub-agent in a fresh context window. In the Warp benchmark shown, an independent reviewer averaged 71.1% correctness at $12.02 vs 68.6% at $4.82 for self-review. • 9:07 Make the reviewer return structured JSON: Have the reviewer output a verdict ("approved" / "needs changes" / "requires human input") plus findings with line/blocks, a suggestion and severity ("nit" / "important" / "critical"). • 11:50 Run the agent review loop before opening the PR: Keep implement/review iterations inside your agent platform so GitHub isn't cluttered with bot comments. • 12:16 Cap implement/review rounds at about 3-5: Limit the agent implement-and-review loop to roughly 3-5 turns. • 20:30 Verify end to end in a sandbox via Chrome DevTools Protocol: A "Test Desktop App" skill boots the Electron app in a container (factory.yaml: os linux, arch x86_64, dockerImage warpdotdev/dev-base:latest) and drives it through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. • 26:45 Have the agent record its test session as an MP4: Give reviewers a video of the agent's verification run. • 28:35 Add a merge-risk skill to every PR: Score the PR on Alignment, Impact, Verification, Rollback cost and Error detection, and append a low/medium/high risk rating to the PR description. (Source: https://youtu.be/uPCH2axUpbc)
